In ChIP-seq experiments some genomic regions (“hyper–ChIP-able” or “phantom” sites) give artifactual peaks for many unrelated antibodies.  
These regions are almost always highly open, heavily transcribed loci such as active promoters and enhancers.  
With only formaldehyde (PFA) cross-linking, loosely or indirectly associated proteins (or even antibody sticking to exposed chromatin) can be pulled down, generating such false-positive peaks.  
Adding a protein–protein cross-linker like DSG strengthens specific cross-linking of the target factor to its genuine binding sites but at the same time reduces recovery of these nonspecific, open-chromatin–driven interactions.  
Therefore the peaks that disappear when PFA+DSG is used are the artifactual peaks at highly open, active regulatory regions.

(A) Introns of large genes – no particular reason for artifactual enrichment  
(B) Random locations – artifacts are not random; they recur at specific open regions  
(C) Repeats – disappearances would be due to mapping issues, not fixation chemistry  
(D) Active promoters and enhancers – characteristic “phantom peak” locations that vanish with stronger cross-linking

Hence, the disappearing peaks are most likely at active promoters and enhancers.

Answer: D
